nodes.content: Design distributed Adam state management supporting elastic resharding and crash recovery without mixing optimizer steps or duplicating updates.
requirements: After any single worker crash during resharding, recover parameters and moments matching uninterrupted deterministic execution.
Limit failure-free step-time overhead to 10% versus static sharding with identical hardware and workloads.

nodes.content: Use epoch-fenced Adam shards, pipelined buddy-replicated step deltas, atomic commit markers, and copy-on-write resharding with idempotent replay.
How should an epoch-fenced shard distinguish committed step deltas from in-flight copies after its owner crashes mid-reshard?
Replicated (epoch, step) commit watermarks and watermark-tagged copies let replacements discard uncommitted deltas and replay committed updates once.
Specify watermark and copy ordering, implement fenced replay, then inject crashes throughout resharding and compare states and step latency.
Run 10,000 seeded single-worker crash injections at copy/commit boundaries; compare bitwise parameters, moments, and applied-step IDs against uninterrupted Adam.
Across 10,000 seeded crashes, recovered parameters and moments matched baseline bitwise; applied-step logs showed zero omissions or duplicates.
Given zero replay mismatches, adopt watermark-tagged copies and replay for correctness; gate deployment on measured failure-free overhead ≤10%.
Implement adopted watermark-tagged replay and conditionally deploy after measuring ≤10% failure-free step overhead versus static sharding.
Benchmark median step time during resharding and steady state against static sharding on identical 8×A100, 1B-parameter workloads.
8×A100 benchmark report: median step times were 420 ms static, 443 ms steady-state (+5.5%), and 450 ms resharding (+7.1%).
Audit the benchmark report with 30 matched 8×A100 reruns, checking median-step confidence intervals and resharding workload parity.
Across 30 matched reruns, resharding median-step overhead was 7.1% (95% CI: 6.2–8.3%); workload parity passed.
Quorum-certified copy manifests and step IDs identify complete snapshots and committed deltas, enabling exactly-once recovery after an owner crash.
Inject 10,000 owner crashes at partial-copy, manifest-certification, and commit boundaries; compare recovered Adam state and applied-step IDs against baseline.
Of 10,000 crashes, 17 certified manifests mixed step-71 parameters with step-70 moments; recovered states diverged despite unique step IDs.
How can copy-on-write resharding certify parameters, both moments, and step counters from one committed Adam step?
Prototype step-pinned copy-on-write bundles; certify manifests only when parameter, moment, and counter tags match one committed step.
StepBundle v1 adds immutable (epoch, step)-tagged parameter, moment, and counter pages; mismatched tags prevent manifest certification.
StepBundle v1 rejected all 17 previously mixed manifests; 10,000 replayed crashes recovered bitwise-matching parameters and moments without duplicate steps.
Replicate ordered gradient batches, checkpoint immutable Adam tuples periodically, and rebuild migrating shards by deterministic replay behind epoch-fenced step tokens.
Implement gradient-log replay and epoch-fenced commits, then test crash recovery against deterministic Adam and benchmark step overhead against static sharding.
Compare StepBundle v1-backed resharding against gradient-log replay on 8×A100, measuring bitwise crash recovery and failure-free overhead versus static sharding.
On 8×A100 sparse-Adam, failure-free overhead versus static was 13.2% for StepBundle, 7.8% for replay; both recovered bitwise.
When can old-epoch gradient logs be truncated without stranding a replacement replaying a partially migrated shard?
Old-epoch logs through step s can be truncated after every migrating shard replicates its step-s checkpoint and fences old ownership.
Using StepBundle v1, inject 10,000 crashes around all-shard checkpoint acknowledgments, ownership fencing, and log truncation; check bitwise recovery.
In 12/10,000 crashes, truncation followed replication and fencing, but missing durable checkpoint-location records stranded replacement replay.
Truncate through step s only after all shards replicate step-s checkpoints, durably publish their locations, and fence old ownership.
Inject 20,000 single-worker crashes around checkpoint-location publication and truncation; verify bitwise Adam recovery and unique committed step IDs.
Across 20,000 injected crashes, durable checkpoint-location publication yielded bitwise Adam recovery, with zero missing or duplicated committed steps.
Adopt gradient-log replay with durable checkpoint-location publication before truncation: 7.8% sparse-Adam overhead and zero mismatches across 20,000 crashes.
Implement durable-location-gated log truncation in ElasticAdam v1; run 8×A100 dense/sparse benchmarks and single-worker resharding crash injections.
ElasticAdam v1 ships epoch-fenced gradient-log replay and durable-location-gated truncation, plus 8×A100 dense/sparse benchmarks and crash-recovery fixtures.
How are gradient batches sequenced across membership changes so replay preserves Adam’s floating-point reduction order and consumes each batch once?
Log fixed-tree reduced-gradient bytes with globally ordered (epoch, step) IDs; fence stale writers and replay each committed ID once.
Replicate immutable Adam shard checkpoints, retain minibatch seeds, and recompute missing fixed-tree gradients under epoch-fenced commits during migration.
Can minibatch seeds reproduce identical gradient bytes after membership changes when worker-local data order and reduction topology change?
Replay seeded minibatches across 8→7-worker resharding; compare sample order, reduction topology, and gradient-byte hashes against uninterrupted execution.
On ElasticAdam v1, compare fixed-tree logged gradients against seed-only recomputation across 8→7 resharding; audit gradient hashes and step IDs.
With fixed sample indices and reduction trees, logged and seed-recomputed gradients matched baseline bytewise across 50,000 8→7 resharded steps.
Keep logged-gradient replay as the recovery default; permit seed recomputation only with persisted sample indices and reduction trees.
Finalize logged-gradient recovery; gate seed fallback on recorded sample indices and reduction trees, then verify single-crash equivalence and ≤10% overhead.
Run ElasticAdam v1 dense/sparse 8×A100 benchmarks and 20,000 single-worker resharding crashes, checking bitwise replay, step-ID uniqueness, and ≤10% overhead.
ElasticAdam v1.1 gates seed fallback on stored sample indices and reduction trees; report records 20,000 bitwise recoveries, 8.4% overhead.
Audit ElasticAdam v1.1 with 30 matched dense/sparse 8×A100 runs and 5,000 crashes; verify overhead and bitwise recovery.
Across 5,000 crashes, checkpoint-seeded recomputation recovered bitwise with pinned samples and trees; 30-run median overhead was 8.4%.
Approve ElasticAdam v1.1 with logged-gradient recovery by default and pinned-sample seed fallback; audited overhead was 8.4% with 5,000 bitwise recoveries.
From StepBundle v1 checkpoints, recompute seeded gradients across 8→7 workers with altered sample orders and reduction trees; compare baseline hashes.
Across 10,000 8→7 replays, seed-only recomputation mismatched 1,204 gradient hashes, including 317 despite fixed reduction trees.
Revise ElasticAdam v1.1: require committed gradient-hash verification before seed fallback; otherwise replay logged bytes to avoid seed-only mismatches.
